evidence_quotes.quote: This paper aims (1) to provide information about the status of water infrastructure in a region of Haiti where records of existing infrastructure are not otherwise accessible; and (2) to explore perceptions of water quality, common barriers to accessing water sources and community-led solutions to water insecurity from the local perspective.

A total of 66 eligible key informants remained from the original 304 individuals who participated in the cultural consensus instrument. Of these 66 eligible informants, 32 women agreed to participate in the follow-up investigation and were subsequently interviewed.

Several women reported their household paying for the installation of a pipe on their property that turned out to be non-functional. Others stated that they were informed that the water could not reach their home due to distance or elevation even if pipes were installed.
Informal and poorly designed water systems in the region were identified as the major barrier to uninterrupted access to water, and intermittency was reported as a greater stressor than quality.

This research focused on the water access issues at the forefront of women’s minds in Gressier, but future research into water governance, resource mapping and negotiations of power, education and myriad other domains are also vital to a holistic understanding of water access in Haiti.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community drinking and domestic water service access (private/shared yard standpipes, community taps, pumps, wells, protected springs, and rainwater) in peri-urban Gressier, Haiti.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper is borderline/weak: it discusses fragmented short-term NGO aid delivery, lack of infrastructure documentation, volunteer/grassroots community source maintenance, and brief participant anecdotes about collective shutoffs for non-payment on informal neighbour-to-neighbour pipes and volunteer pump caretakers locking pumps, though the authors explicitly state in Future Directions (p. 916) that water governance was outside their focus and left for future research. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification, Criterion 2 is clearly not met (no): the study investigates physical/topographical and infrastructural barriers (gravity pressure loss across informal neighbour-to-neighbour PVC extensions, seasonality/flooding, distance, post-surgical physical limits), water quality/chlorination perceptions, and generic NGO project sustainability/community self-help rather than analysing any legal, administrative, regulatory, eligibility, tenure, or formal tariff/enforcement rule governing service access.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary qualitative empirical evidence from semi-structured in-depth household interviews and ethnographic source visits (March-April 2018) with 32 women selected from a 304-participant cultural consensus survey sample, coded thematically in NVivo.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative household water access outcomes including non-functional pipe installations, service intermittency and schedule disruptions, shutoffs, wait times, reliance on distant or lower-quality sources, and collection hardships.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the study population and unit of analysis (32 adult/adolescent women in households in Gressier, Haiti), infrastructural/environmental barriers examined, household water access outcomes, and qualitative ethnographic study design (though it lacks an eligible rule-type legal/administrative exposure under Criterion 2).
criterion_notes.c6: Published in English (interviews conducted in Haitian Kreyol and translated into English for analysis and reporting).

study_design: Qualitative study (semi-structured in-depth interviews and ethnographic investigation following cultural consensus screening)
population_and_sample: Women over 16 years of age residing in Gressier, Ouest department, Haiti (n = 32 key informants interviewed at the household level, selected from 66 eligible high-consensus respondents out of a 304-participant survey sample)
exposure: Physical and infrastructural water barriers (elevation/low gravity pressure, informal neighbour-to-neighbour PVC pipe dispersion, seasonality/flooding, distance/terrain, post-surgical physical limitations), NGO aid project discontinuity, and informal community source maintenance
outcome: Lived experiences of household water access, piped water functionality and intermittency, collection hardships and wait times, and perceived water quality and household treatment
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). While this qualitative ethnographic study empirically examines household water service access and intermittency among 32 women in Gressier, Haiti, its exposure focus is physical/topographical infrastructure limitations (low gravity pressure, neighbour-to-neighbour PVC pipe dispersion, flooding/seasonality, physical health barriers), water quality/treatment perceptions, short-term NGO project sustainability, and grassroots community self-help. Per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification, generic WASH project delivery/maintenance gaps and unanalysed governance background do not constitute a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism governing service access, and the authors explicitly note that water governance was left for future research.
